One mechanism, several ways to check the model

I want to understand why a controller produces a command, and whether its mathematics agrees with the mechanism.

The work progressed from geometric Python IK to analytical C++ kinematics and an independent transform-based derivation. Along the way I changed coordinate conventions, checked derivatives, and separated numerical model consistency from physical tracking.

From sketches to differential kinematics

The connection between position and velocity
p = f(q)
vfoot = J(q)q̇
J(q) = ∂f / ∂q

The Jacobian is the derivative of a particular model under a particular convention. Signs, zero angles, length units, and the chosen leg frame are part of that definition.

Body orientation and feedback

I studied geometric torso correction, quaternion and axis-angle error, and the motion of feet expressed in a rotating body frame. These notes connect an orientation error to a desired foot correction, then to joint motion through the leg model.

A velocity expressed in a rotating frame
vfoot,world = vbody,world + R(vfoot,body + ωbody × rfoot,body)

Here ω and r use the body frame, and R rotates body-frame vectors into the world frame. This is a kinematic relationship; it does not establish a validated whole-body dynamics controller.

What the saved numerical checks say

The retained October 18, 2026 MATLAB study compares the same leg model through homogeneous transforms, symbolic derivatives, geometric Jacobian columns, and numerical perturbations.

6,000sampled configurations
9.65 × 10−11maximum Jacobian finite-difference difference · m/rad
1.76 × 10−16maximum IK position round-trip error · m

Saved offline results for a recorded model and source snapshot. They were inspected, rather than rerun for this website update. Some current controller files have changed since that snapshot. These values describe numerical consistency, not physical tracking accuracy.

CAD mass and inertia

A CAD export can have the right shape and still omit mass-bearing components. I worked through component accounting, center of mass, inertia orientation, and frame conventions before using the model as a dynamics foundation.

An earlier corrected simulation snapshot has 13 links, 12 moving joints, and 12.54 kg of CAD-derived mass. That number describes this model and component snapshot; it is not a measured weight for every physical robot revision.

Rotate and shift each component inertia
Itotal = Σ [RiIiRiᵀ + mi((di·di)I − didiᵀ)]

Each component inertia is rotated into a common frame, then shifted to the aggregate center of mass with the parallel-axis theorem. The component masses are accounted for directly rather than scaled by a single global factor.

verify_mass_correction.py · inertia aggregationPython / NumPy
axes = b.ximat[index].reshape(3, 3)
delta = b.xipos[index] - center
inertia += axes @ np.diag(new.body_inertia[index]) @ axes.T
inertia += new.body_mass[index] * (
    np.dot(delta, delta) * np.eye(3) - np.outer(delta, delta)
)

Control and learning: the next questions

My independent study includes PD system behavior, state estimation, LQR, centroidal MPC, and PPO. I am interested in testing where a learned correction can improve an understandable conventional baseline. That remains a development direction, rather than a demonstrated hybrid controller.

WHAT THIS ESTABLISHES

Model and learning infrastructure; behavioral validation remains separate.

The simulation and policy pipeline support further experiments. Existing smoke-policy checks do not establish learned walking, trotting, robust terrain traversal, or sim-to-real transfer. LQR and MPC notes are study and preliminary formulation work.
